## Web Development Company in Pune: Who Has the Keys to Your WordPress Site? A Plain Guide to Admin Users, Two-Factor Login and Offboarding Former Staff and Agencies

Most hacked or damaged WordPress sites are not broken by clever attackers; they are opened with a key somebody forgot they had handed out. A former developer who still has an Administrator login, a shared password pinned in a WhatsApp group, an intern account nobody deleted: these are the doors that actually get used. A good web development company in Pune will review who can log in to your site in the first week of any project and will leave you with a written list of who holds which key. This guide shows you how to do that review yourself, which WordPress roles to give to which people, how to switch on two-factor login, and what to do the day somebody leaves.

You do not need to be technical. You need a list of people, a short set of rules and about an hour. The article walks through the problem, the five standard WordPress roles, an audit you can run today, two-factor login choices, a clean offboarding routine, and the clauses to put in an agency contract so access never depends on one person's memory.

## Why access, not code, is the usual weak point

A WordPress site has three layers of access, and most owners only think about one. The first is the WordPress dashboard (the `/wp-admin` login). The second is the hosting account, where files, databases and backups live. The third is everything connected to the site: the domain registrar, email service, payment gateway, analytics, Search Console and any plugin licences. Somebody with the dashboard Administrator role can install a plugin, and a plugin can do almost anything on the server, so an Administrator login is effectively a master key to the site.

Several realistic scenarios show how this goes wrong:

- **The departed freelancer.** A freelancer built the site two years ago, shared a login by email and moved on. The account is still an Administrator with a weak password reused on other services. When that password appears in a breach elsewhere, the site is exposed.
- **The shared login.** Three marketing staff use one account called `admin`. When something is changed or deleted, nobody can say who did it, and when one person leaves the password is not changed because "everyone knows it".
- **The over-trusted helper.** A content writer is made an Administrator "just to make things easier" and accidentally deactivates a plugin that runs the checkout.
- **The forgotten test account.** An account created for a vendor's demo is never removed.

None of these needs a technical attack. They need an hour of housekeeping, which is why this is one of the cheapest security improvements available to a small business or NGO. If you are also worried about plugins and server-side hardening, see our companion guides on [auditing WordPress plugins](/blog/web-development-company-pune-wordpress-plugin-audit-abandoned-plugins-2026) and [HTTP security headers](/blog/web-development-company-pune-http-security-headers-hsts-csp-2026); this article is about people.

## The five WordPress roles in plain language

WordPress ships with five standard roles on a single site. Giving each person the lowest role that lets them do their job is called the principle of least privilege, and it limits the damage any single mistake or stolen password can cause.

| Role | What the person can do | Typical person |
|---|---|---|
| Administrator | Everything: install and delete plugins and themes, add and remove users, change site settings | One or two trusted owners, plus your developer while working |
| Editor | Publish and manage all posts and pages, including other people's; moderate comments | Head of content or communications |
| Author | Publish and manage only their own posts | Regular blog writer |
| Contributor | Write posts but not publish them; cannot upload images by default | Guest writer, volunteer, intern |
| Subscriber | Manage their own profile only | Members or registered readers |

On a WordPress Multisite network there is also a Super Admin, who controls the whole network. Most small business sites are not multisite, so you can ignore it unless your developer says otherwise.

Plugins can add roles of their own. A WooCommerce store adds a Shop Manager and Customer role; some form, LMS and membership plugins add more. Shop Manager is a good example of least privilege done well: the person can handle orders and products without being able to install code on the site. When a plugin adds roles, read what each role can do before assigning it, because the names are not always self-explanatory.

### A simple mapping that works for most Indian small businesses

- **Owner or director:** one Administrator account in their own name, protected with two-factor login, used rarely.
- **Developer or agency:** an Administrator account in the named developer's own name, active only while work is under way.
- **Marketing or content staff:** Editor or Author.
- **Shop staff on a store:** Shop Manager.
- **Volunteers, interns and guest writers:** Contributor.
- **Everyone else:** no account at all.

Two Administrators is a sensible ceiling for most organisations. One is risky because the only person who can manage the site may be unreachable; five is a lot of master keys to protect.

## A one-hour access audit you can run today

Open the dashboard and go to **Users > All Users**. You are going to build a short register in a spreadsheet. The goal is that every account maps to a named human who still needs it.

### Step 1: List every account

For each user write down the username, display name, email address, role and last login if your security plugin records it. WordPress itself does not show last-login dates; a security or activity-log plugin does. If you have none, you can still judge by asking each person whether they use the account.

### Step 2: Match accounts to people

Anything you cannot match to a current person is a candidate for removal. Watch for these warning signs:

- Usernames such as `admin`, `administrator`, `test`, `demo` or a company name. Generic usernames are guessed first in automated login attempts.
- Email addresses at domains you do not recognise, or at an old agency's domain.
- Several people sharing one account.
- Accounts whose display name differs from the person using them.

### Step 3: Downgrade, then delete

Where someone has a higher role than they need, change it to the correct role. Where an account belongs to no one, delete it. When WordPress asks what to do with that user's content, choose **Attribute all content to** a current user so posts and pages are not lost. If you are unsure whether an account is in use, you can first downgrade it to Subscriber for a week and see whether anyone complains; this is safer than deleting immediately.

### Step 4: Check the less visible keys

The user list is only the front door. Also check:

- **Hosting account users.** Most hosting control panels let you add and remove team members and list SSH or FTP accounts. Remove old FTP users and any account in a former agency's name.
- **Application passwords.** WordPress lets users create application passwords (added in version 5.6) so that an external app can connect to the site. Open each administrator's profile page and review the Application Passwords section; revoke any you do not recognise.
- **Plugin and API keys.** Payment, email and analytics integrations often store keys in the plugin settings. If an ex-employee had access to those screens, treat the keys as known to them and rotate the important ones.
- **Third-party accounts.** Google Search Console, Google Analytics, Tag Manager, Meta Business Manager and your domain registrar each have their own user lists. People who left often still appear there. Our [website handover checklist](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026) covers who should own each of these.
- **Email accounts on your domain.** A departed employee's mailbox can be used to reset passwords for other services, so deal with it in the same exercise.

### Step 5: Save the register

The register should record the account, the person, the role, the reason they need it and the date you last reviewed it. Store it where more than one trusted person can find it. Repeat the review quarterly; it takes far less time the second time.

## Passwords: the minimum that actually helps

Strong, unique passwords still matter, and a password manager is the realistic way to achieve them. Several rules are worth stating plainly:

1. Use a different password for every account, particularly for the WordPress dashboard and hosting. Reuse is how a breach at an unrelated website becomes a breach of yours.
2. Prefer long passphrases generated by a password manager to short complex ones that people write on sticky notes.
3. Never share a login by email, WhatsApp or SMS if you can avoid it. If a one-off share is unavoidable, change the password afterwards. A better route is a team password manager that lets you share an entry and revoke it later.
4. Give each person their own account, so that activity can be traced and one person's departure does not force everyone to change a password.
5. Do not let browsers on shared computers remember dashboard passwords.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology's digital identity guidelines (SP 800-63B) explain the reasoning behind length-based passwords and breached-password checks, and CERT-In publishes general cyber-hygiene advice for Indian users; both are worth a read if you want the technical background. ## Two-factor login: what it is and which kind to choose

Two-factor authentication (2FA) asks for a second proof after the password, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get in. WordPress core does not include 2FA, so you add it with a well-maintained plugin or through your host or a security service. The common options differ in convenience and strength.

| Method | How it works | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Authenticator app (TOTP) | A six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds, generated by an app on the phone | Free, works offline, widely supported | Codes can still be typed into a fake login page; losing the phone needs a recovery plan |
| SMS code | A code sent by text message | Familiar to users | Weakest of the options; messages can be diverted by SIM-swap fraud and need mobile coverage |
| Email code | A code sent to the user's inbox | No extra app | Only as safe as the mailbox; useless if the mailbox shares the same password |
| Passkey or security key | A cryptographic credential held on a device, checked against the exact website | Resistant to fake login pages; no code to type | Needs plugin and browser support; recovery and device changes need planning |
| Backup codes | One-time codes printed or saved in advance | Essential recovery route | Must be stored safely, since each is a master key |

For most small organisations, an authenticator app is the sensible default, with backup codes stored in the company password manager. Passkeys are a stronger option where your plugin supports them and your team's devices are modern; our article on [passkeys and passwordless authentication](/blog/web-development-company-pune-passkeys-authentication-2026) explains the trade-offs in more depth.

### Who must use 2FA

Require it for every Administrator and Editor first, as they can change the most. Then extend it to Shop Manager and anyone who can see customer or donor data. Subscribers and customers generally should not be forced into 2FA unless there is a reason, because it adds friction for people who can do little harm.

### Make it a rule, not a request

A plugin that lets users opt in leaves your weakest account unprotected. Choose a plugin that can enforce 2FA by role, with a short grace period for people to enrol. Before enforcing, make sure each person has stored backup codes, and make sure two Administrators exist so the loss of one phone does not lock you out of your own site.

### Plan for the locked-out administrator

Write down, before you need it, how access is recovered if every Administrator loses their second factor. Typically it involves the developer or host disabling the 2FA plugin through the hosting file manager or the database, which is why the hosting account must be under your control. If recovery depends on one freelancer who has left, 2FA can turn a minor inconvenience into a site lock-out.


## Offboarding: what to do the day someone leaves

Offboarding is the moment the whole system is tested. A same-day routine for an employee, freelancer or agency avoids almost every access problem.

### Offboarding checklist for a person

1. **Disable or downgrade their WordPress account** on the day of departure. Delete it once content has been reassigned.
2. **Revoke hosting, FTP and SSH access** and remove them from the hosting control panel.
3. **Remove them from third-party tools:** Search Console, Analytics, Tag Manager, ad accounts, Meta Business Manager, email marketing and payment dashboards.
4. **Rotate shared secrets they knew:** any shared password, API key or payment-gateway key. This is the step most often skipped.
5. **Reassign their email forwarding and mailbox** so that password-reset emails do not reach a former employee.
6. **Collect licences and assets:** theme and plugin licence keys, design files, content drafts and documentation.
7. **Update the register** and record the date.
8. **Tell the team** who now owns their responsibilities, so that nobody keeps using a colleague's login to "get things done".

### Offboarding an agency or freelancer

When you move to a new developer, treat the old one's accounts the same way, but plan the handover so that the site is never left without a person who can fix it. A sound sequence is:

1. Agree the handover date in writing and ask the outgoing party for an inventory of every account, licence and credential they hold.
2. Bring the new developer on with their own named Administrator account.
3. Confirm that you, the owner, are the registered contact on the domain, hosting and plugin licences.
4. Take a full backup before any access is removed, and confirm you can restore it. See our guide to [website backups and disaster recovery](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-backups-disaster-recovery-2026).
5. Remove the old party's access on the agreed date, and rotate secrets they knew.
6. Ask for written confirmation that they have deleted local copies of your data where that applies.

Good agencies do this willingly. If a developer is reluctant to hand over credentials or insists on keeping accounts "for support", treat that as a warning about the working relationship.

## What to put in an agency or freelancer contract

Access should be covered in writing so that it does not depend on goodwill. Useful clauses include:

- **Ownership of accounts.** Domain, hosting, plugin licences and third-party accounts are registered in the client's name.
- **Named individual accounts.** Developers use personal accounts, never a shared login, so that activity is traceable.
- **Least privilege.** The developer holds Administrator access only for the duration of the work, and a lower role for ongoing support if that is enough.
- **Two-factor login.** Accounts with high-level access use 2FA.
- **Credential handling.** Passwords are shared through a password manager, not through email or messaging apps.
- **Offboarding and handover.** On termination the developer returns an inventory, removes their access and cooperates in handover, within a stated number of days.
- **Incident notice.** The developer informs you promptly if they believe a credential has been exposed.
- **Data handling.** Where the site holds customer or donor data, the contract states what the developer may access, for what purpose and for how long. Our guide to [DPDP Act compliance for websites](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-pune-2026) explains why this matters for personal data.

If you are choosing a new developer, our [shortlist of questions to ask a web development company](/blog/web-development-company-pune-shortlist-questions-2026) includes access and handover alongside price and timeline.

## A worked example: a small Pune clinic

Consider a hypothetical clinic in Pune with a WordPress site and an appointment form. Over four years the site has been touched by three freelancers and two front-desk staff. An audit finds six Administrators, two of them with generic usernames, plus an FTP account in a former agency's name.

A sensible clean-up looks like this:

1. The owner and the current developer remain Administrators, each with a personal account and an authenticator app.
2. The practice manager becomes an Editor.
3. The two generic accounts and the former freelancers' accounts are deleted, with content reassigned to the practice manager.
4. The old FTP account is removed from the host and the hosting password is changed.
5. The appointment form's email notifications are checked, since a former staff member's address was still receiving patient enquiries; the address is replaced with a monitored shared mailbox.
6. A one-page register is created and a quarterly reminder is set.

No technical change to the site itself was needed; the exercise took an afternoon. The point of this example is its ordinariness: most small organisations have a similar mess, and the fix is housekeeping rather than expensive security software. The clinic and its numbers are illustrative only and do not describe a real client.

## When to bring in a professional

You can do the audit yourself, but ask a developer to help when:

- you cannot tell which accounts are in use and fear removing something that matters;
- your site holds sensitive data such as health, financial or donor records;
- you suspect an account has already been misused, for example unknown administrators appearing or content changing on its own;
- you want 2FA enforced by role, an activity log and login limits configured and tested together.

If you suspect a compromise, change passwords from a clean device, force a log-out of all sessions (a user can do this from their profile with the option to log out everywhere else), review recently installed plugins and recent file changes, and restore from a clean backup if needed. Keep evidence, and where personal data may have been exposed, take advice on your legal reporting duties. For Indian organisations that includes checking obligations under the DPDP Act and, for certain incidents, CERT-In reporting directions. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many Administrator accounts should a WordPress site have?

Usually two: one for the owner and one for the developer who maintains the site. One leaves you exposed if that person is unavailable; many more increase the number of master keys to protect. Everyone else should hold a lower role such as Editor or Author.

### Can I share one WordPress login with my team?

You should not. Shared logins make it impossible to trace changes, and a departure forces everyone to change the password. Give each person an account with the lowest role they need, and share secrets through a password manager if you must share them at all.

### Does WordPress have two-factor authentication built in?

No. WordPress core does not include it, so you need a reputable plugin, a host feature or a security service. Choose one that is actively maintained, can enforce 2FA by role and supports authenticator apps or passkeys, and keep backup codes in a safe place.

### What should I do when a developer or employee leaves?

On the day they leave, disable their WordPress account, remove their hosting and third-party access, and change any shared password or key they knew. Then update your access register. Delaying this step is the most common reason former staff still have access years later.

### How often should I review who can log in to my site?

Quarterly is a sensible rhythm for most small organisations, and immediately after any change of developer, agency or key staff. The first review takes about an hour; later reviews are much shorter.

Sources: [WordPress.org: Roles and Capabilities](https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/roles-and-capabilities/), [WordPress.org: Application Passwords (WordPress 5.6 field guide)](https://make.wordpress.org/core/2020/11/05/application-passwords-integration-guide/), [WordPress.org: Hardening WordPress](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/security/hardening/), [NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html), [CERT-In](https://www.cert-in.org.in/). Plugin features and policy details change; confirm them against current documentation before relying on them.
